P1.evidence: The rep handled a hostile pre-frame extremely well, which is the best thing on the call. The prospect opened by pre-empting the whole sales process and the rep neither pushed back nor caved: 'at the end of the day, it's not, it's your decision, not mine' and 'I don't want to sell you something that's not aligned with you at all... maybe there is a hypothesis that this isn't for you.' But the frame he set was two-part, not four — 'Let's just go. A few questions, and if there's an alignment, I will show you which one, which program that Trevor has would be suited for you' — with no where-you-are, where-you-want-to-go, what's-in-the-way, what-you-need structure. Frame agreement was asked and given ('Is that perfect?' / 'Yeah'). The open question landed cleanly: 'brief me in, like, what's goal that you want to actually achieve?' Setter notes were used once in passing ('Do I remember correctly that you're building a startup right now?') but never read back at the open.

P2.evidence: The health screen was the most complete in the batch and was run properly: 'Do you have any limitations, any injuries whatsoever?', then the sharper follow-up 'any injuries that are affecting your day-to-day life right now that may be a limitation to your workout?', then 'Any other chronic conditions that are in the family or something like that?'. Nutrition was asked directly with a good comfort-food probe. Work and desk-bound status were established, though the substantive question — 'Mind asking what kind of startup are you building?' — was asked after the payment had been taken. Age, height and weight were never asked or given at all, which for a programme selling loaded ballistic training is a real omission. Results from current training, sleep and energy were all skipped. Training frequency was only half-established: twenty years of daily training is on record, but what he actually does in a week is not.

P3.evidence: The rep asked the surface goal twice and got a flat answer — 'Apart from the sustainability, what are you trying to achieve, actually? Like, is there any specific, like, health goal?' / 'No, no.' He then stopped. There was no bridge to what is driving it, no question about who else it impacts, and no drive through to marriage, identity or legacy despite a wife being mentioned twice. The rep actively closed the door: 'it's basically having something that is sustainable and that you can adapt in your lifestyle when you travel and just for health and longevity was not, nothing, nothing more.' That summary is a reflect-back of the surface want, not of a deeper why, so P3h scores partial at best. Material was sitting there untouched — 'I work out because it feels good mentally' and 'it's how I want to start my day' are the beginning of an identity thread that was never pulled.

P4.evidence: The only past-attempts question was narrow and about modality — 'did you do any kettlebell workouts before?' — not about what he has tried and what happened. The prospect volunteered the entire root cause unprompted twenty minutes in, after the pillars and while waiting for a price: 'My problem is, I don't want to think... There's nobody specialized... You can hire a trainer anywhere. They all do the same.' The rep did not ask a single follow-up on it. He also volunteered 'I've done many online programs. I've done it all' and a specific bad experience — 'I tried this program online, and they sold me on, you can still eat whatever you want' — and neither was explored. Per the scoring rule, information the prospect volunteers and the rep never asks for is a miss.

P5.evidence: Not attempted in any form. No two-year question, no test of willingness to settle, no line in the sand. It was reachable — the call ran 32 minutes with time to spare — and the rep simply moved from the pillar presentation toward price when the prospect pushed for it.

P6.evidence: Three comprehension checks were run — 'is that something that you can fit in your schedule?', 'Does that make sense?', 'What questions would you have on that?' — and they produced a good answer on frequency ('I want to get at least five days, you know, four days I think is reasonable'). None of them is the belief question the script asks for. The all-in check was never asked in any form. The genuine verbal yes that phase 6 exists to obtain was never sought before presenting; the prospect supplied it himself by demanding the price.

P11.evidence: The two hard steps ran cleanly and in the right order. Payment first — link into the Zoom chat, prospect paid live, rep verified: 'okay paid oh okay let me just double check yep'. Onboarding with Trevor booked only after that, for 11:15am the next day, which matches the internal rule about not putting unpaid people on Trevor's calendar. The agreement was sent and its arrival confirmed, but it was not signed on the call — the rep offered 'If you don't have time right now, you can do it later today' and, when the prospect said he would not read it, replied 'Exactly.' The welcome email, Skool link and onboarding form were all covered, but Skool was described to a full-price client as the place for people who cannot afford coaching: 'if someone doesn't have the budget and wants to, like, do it on their own or something like that, he can learn from that.'

objection_plays.detail: The trigger was a structure preference rather than an affordability problem — 'I like it but I can't pay monthly... I would prefer to pay monthly.' The rep skipped every scripted move: no isolation, no should-I-versus-how frame, no permission question about an open financial conversation, and not one item of the financial picture. He went straight to a four-option menu, then reversed the prospect's chosen option to full payment with 'No, but half, in 30 days, it means nothing. It's the same thing.' It worked, and the scripted play was not the reason.

Gap in the script: the prospect opened with an explicit anti-sales pre-frame — 'I don't do the hard sell. I do it on my terms... I'm here to get educated. And if I like it, it sounds great.' There is no play for a buyer who declares the process invalid before it starts. The rep improvised well: he validated it, ceded control ('it's your decision, not mine'), and offered his own disqualification hypothesis. The prospect rewarded it immediately — 'I'm here because I'm sold, by the way' and 'that's one star for me so far.' This improvisation is worth writing into the playbook.

Gap in the script: a live technique-and-discomfort concern — 'when I do snatches, sometimes when the kettlebell hits my forearm, it's a little uncomfortable.' There is no scripted handling for a prospect raising a physical discomfort during a movement the programme centres on. The rep coached the technique remotely and deferred to Trevor, and never connected it to the broken wrist the prospect had disclosed twelve minutes earlier.

notes: This is the textbook sloppy-call-that-closed and it should be scored as such. Phases 3, 4, 5 and 6 — 75 of the 120 available weight — were essentially not run. The prospect did the discovery on the rep's behalf, named his own root cause unprompted, and demanded the price twice. What the rep genuinely did well is worth keeping: he defused an anti-sales pre-frame better than the playbook knows how to, he ran the most complete injury and family-history screen in the batch, and his P11 sequencing was correct. Two things to correct. First, when a buyer hands you 'My problem is, I don't want to think' and 'there's no one really focused and specialized', that is the root cause arriving late — stop and work it, because a closed deal with no articulated why is a churn risk at month three. Second, the six-month instalment option was quoted as '1,200 a month' with the $7,200 total never spoken aloud.
